teach.title: Latin has no word for 'that'
teach.say: English reports with a joining word: *she sees that the boy is sleeping*. Latin has none, and uses **the accusative + infinitive (the 'that …' clause after says / sees / thinks)** instead, *accūsātīvus cum īnfīnītīvō*: the reported person goes into the accusative (the object form) and the reported verb into the infinitive (the 'to' form). *Syra puerum dormīre videt* — literally Syra sees the-boy-to-sleep.

teach.title: The accusative word is the one doing it
teach.say: This is the step that feels wrong at first. *Puerum* looks like an object, but nobody is doing anything to the boy — he is the one asleep. Inside a reported clause the accusative is the *subject*, and the infinitive is its verb: *avem canere* = the bird is singing, *līberōs lūdere* = the children are playing. Ask who does the infinitive's action and the accusative answers.

teach.title: What sets it off
teach.say: The pattern is set off by a verb of seeing, hearing, saying or thinking, and in these chapters that means *videt* (sees) and *audit* (hears). That verb usually comes last, after the whole reported clause: *Quīntus canem in viā lātrāre audit*. It need not: *Mārcus videt Iūliam rosās carpere* puts it second and *Audit Syra Quīntum in cubiculō plōrāre* puts it first. Find the reporting verb before you translate, wherever it stands.

teach.title: esse in the clause, and being-done verbs
teach.say: If what is reported is a state, the infinitive is *esse*, and any adjective in the clause agrees with the accusative subject: *Quīntum vīvum esse videt* = sees that Quintus is alive — *Quīntum* and *vīvum* both accusative. If what is reported is done to somebody, the infinitive turns passive: *sē ā patre vocārī audit* = hears that he is being called by his father.

teach.title: A plain 'to' form, or a reported clause?
teach.say: After *vult*, *potest* and *audet* the infinitive has no subject of its own: *Mārcus dormīre vult* = Marcus wants to sleep — the wanter and the sleeper are the same person. In a reported clause an extra accusative supplies a different doer: *Quīntum canere audit* = he hears that Quintus is singing. Count the accusatives: one that the infinitive itself acts on is an object; one that acts is a reported subject.

core.text: After a verb of saying, seeing or thinking, Latin does not say *that he is sleeping*. It uses **the accusative + infinitive (the 'that …' clause after says / sees / thinks)**: the person reported goes into the accusative (the object form) and the verb into the infinitive (the 'to' form). *Medicus puerum dormīre videt* — the doctor sees the-boy-to-sleep: sees that the boy is sleeping. Latin does it after *videt* (sees), *audit* (hears), *dīcit* (says), *putat* (thinks). Latin name: accūsātīvus cum īnfīnītīvō.

A clause is a small sentence inside a sentence, with its own subject and verb: *I know [that she is here]*. *I saw her run* has an object-form subject (*her*) and a bare verb (*run*) — the Latin shape.
Reported subject in the accusative, reported verb in the infinitive; no word for 'that'.

invented.en: Syra says that the boy is sleeping.
Marcus thinks that he is ill.

core.text: A plain infinitive after *vult* (wants) has no subject of its own: *puer dormīre vult* — the boy wants to sleep. In the accusative + infinitive an extra accusative does the action: *puerum dormīre videt*. Ask who does the infinitive's action; an accusative word means a reported clause.

more.text: The infinitive's tense is relative to the main verb. The present infinitive means 'at the same time': *eum dormīre dīcit* — says he is sleeping; *eum dormīre dīxit* — said he was sleeping. The perfect infinitive (the 'to have done' form) reports something earlier: *eum dormīvisse dīcit* — says he slept.

When the reported person is the same as the speaker, Latin uses *sē* (himself, herself): Quintus says *sē aegrum esse* — that he (Quintus) is ill; *eum aegrum esse* would mean someone else. A passive infinitive works too: *Dāvus Quīntum in lectō pōnī videt* — Davus sees Quintus being put in bed.

The learner's notes (week 10) set two English 'that'-clauses side by side — the indicative (the plain statement form) kind, *I know that she is here*, and the infinitive kind (*I know her to be…*) — and point out that Classical Latin almost always prefers the infinitive kind, while the Vulgate and medieval texts often write *quod / quia / quoniam* + indicative (*videt quod is aedificat*). Use the classical way in composition; expect the other in later readings. The notes' practice set turns direct speech into reported speech: *Aemilia: 'Quīntus vīvus est'* → *Aemilia Quīntum vīvum esse dīcit*.

Ørberg (chapter XI) lists the verbs that take it: *vidēre, audīre, sentīre* (feel, notice), *iubēre*, *dīcere*, *putāre*, *gaudēre* (be glad) and *necesse esse* (*puerum dormīre necesse est* — the boy must sleep). A&G add that an adjective in the clause agrees with its accusative subject (*Quīntum vīvum esse*), and that after *iubeō* the accusative is felt as the object of the ordering as well.
